titulo: Sounds, alphabet and first words: Sounds that English does not have

aula.objetivo: Spell in French, recognize the sounds that English does not have (u, eu, nasal vowels, r), understand silent letters, liaison and elision, and say your first greetings.

sessao.titulo: Sounds that English does not have

blocos.titulo: Three sounds that English does not have: «u», «eu» and «r»
blocos.explicacao: Listen first: «tu», «rue», «deux», «merci». STEP 1: the French «u». Say «ee» and keep your tongue still, right at the front of your mouth. Now round your lips, as if you were about to whistle. Out comes the French «u», which we write here as «ew». It is in «tu» (tew), «rue» (rew) and «salut» (sa-LEW). STEP 2: careful. The French «u» is not the «oo» of «food». The sound of «oo» in «food» is written «ou» in French: «vous» (voo), «bonjour» (bohn-ZHOOR). STEP 3: the «eu» sound. Say «ay» and round your lips, as if to say «oh». Out comes the sound of «deux» (duh), «peu» (puh) and «sœur» (suhr). STEP 4: the French «r» sits in the throat. Think of a gentle gargle: it is not the English «r» of «red», and not a tapped «r» either (like the «r» in Spanish pero). Practice: «rue», «merci», «rouge».
blocos.comparacao: English has no equivalent of «ew» or «uh». So English speakers tend to swap the French «u» for the «oo» of «food», and «eu» for «ay» or a flat «uh». The «r» is the trickiest: if you say it with the English «r» of «red», it will sound foreign. Try a soft gargle from the back of the throat, as if clearing it very gently.

tabela.how: lips as for «oo», tongue as for «ee»
lips as for «oh», tongue as for «ay»
in the throat, like a soft «gargle» (the «r»)
tabela.mistake: English "r" with the tongue curled back

erros.motivo: Lips as for «oh», tongue as for «ay».

erros.errado: saying the English r for the «r» of «rue»
erros.motivo: The French «r» is not made with the tongue.

blocos.explicacao: Listen first: «bon», «pain», «enfant», «hôtel». STEP 1: the nasal vowels. The air comes out through your nose, and your tongue touches nothing. English has no true nasal vowels of its own (the vowels of «ban», «sing» and «sun» only pick up a slight nasal colour), so train your ear. STEP 2: in French there are three main nasal sounds. «on» sounds like «ohn»: «bon», «bonjour». «an» and «en» sound like «ahn»: «enfant», «France». «in», «ain» and «un» sound like «an» (as in "ant", without pronouncing the n): «pain», «vin», «matin». STEP 3: after the nasal vowel, the «n» or «m» is not pronounced as a consonant. Say «bohn» with no real n, and not «bom» or «bon-uh». STEP 4: the «h» is never pronounced. «Hôtel» sounds like «oh-TEHL». STEP 5: the unaccented «e» at the end of a syllable is weak, almost a puff of air, and sometimes it disappears: «je», «le», «petite».
blocos.comparacao: The typical English-speaker mistake is to close the nasal vowel with an «n» or an «m» (or an "ng") that French does not have, saying "bonn" or "bong". Let the air flow through the nose and leave the consonant out.

tabela.how: ahn, with no «n» sound at the end
ohn, with no «m» sound at the end
an, with no «n» sound at the end

erros.errado: pronouncing the final n of bon («bonn»)
erros.motivo: The vowel is nasal, but the «n» does not become a consonant.
The three letters «ain» form a single nasal vowel.

blocos.titulo: À la boulangerie / At the bakery
blocos.ru: C'est le matin, à Paris. Lucas arrive à la boulangerie. La vendeuse dit : « Bonjour, monsieur ! » Lucas répond : « Bonjour, madame ! Un pain, s'il vous plaît. » La vendeuse dit : « Voilà ! » Lucas dit : « Merci. » La vendeuse dit : « De rien. Au revoir ! » Lucas dit : « Au revoir ! » Il est content : le pain est bon !
blocos.pt: It is morning in Paris. Lucas arrives at the bakery. The shop assistant says: «Good morning, sir!» Lucas replies: «Good morning, madam! A loaf of bread, please.» The assistant says: «Here you are!» Lucas says: «Thank you.» The assistant says: «You're welcome. Bye!» Lucas says: «Bye!» He is happy: the bread is good!

perguntas.pergunta: Where does Lucas arrive, and at what time of day?
perguntas.resposta: At the bakery («boulangerie»), in the morning, in Paris.
A loaf of bread: «un pain, s'il vous plaît».

perguntas.pergunta: What does the shop assistant answer when Lucas says «merci»?

blocos.enunciado: Say five times, slowly and then faster: «Un bon pain. Deux rues. Tu as du pain.» Then repeat, like Lucas: «Bonjour, madame ! Un pain, s'il vous plaît. Merci. Au revoir !»
Without looking, say «bonjour», «bonsoir», «merci» and «au revoir». Then spell the name of your city in French.
